title: Pathophysiology: Sodium & Water Disorders—Hyponatremia, Hypernatremia and Brain Adaptation
html:
Serum sodium is a concentration: it describes sodium in relation to water, not simply how much sodium is stored in the body. Most sodium disorders are therefore disorders of water balance. The immediate danger is often neurologic because extracellular tonicity changes move water into or out of brain cells. Safe nursing judgment connects the sodium trend with symptom severity, time course, glucose and osmolality, volume status, urine studies, medications, intake and losses.

Learning goals

  • Explain why serum sodium reflects the water-to-sodium relationship.
  • Differentiate hypotonic, isotonic, and hypertonic hyponatremia.
  • Compare hypovolemic, euvolemic, and hypervolemic patterns.
  • Explain brain-cell swelling in hyponatremia and shrinkage in hypernatremia.
  • Relate ADH excess or deficiency, kidney function, thirst, and access to water to sodium disorders.
  • Recognize severe neurologic cues and initiate seizure and emergency precautions.
  • Explain why sodium correction requires a controlled prescription, serial laboratory monitoring, and assessment for overcorrection.

Start with tonicity—not the sodium number alone

Hyponatremia is commonly defined as serum sodium below 135 mEq/L, and hypernatremia as above 145 mEq/L, though the laboratory's range applies. A reported low sodium should first be interpreted with measured or clinically evaluated serum osmolality and glucose. Most clinically important hyponatremia is hypotonic, meaning extracellular fluid has reduced effective solute concentration and water tends to enter cells.

Marked hyperglycemia can draw water from cells into extracellular fluid and lower measured sodium while tonicity is elevated. Rare laboratory methods may report pseudohyponatremia when extreme lipid or protein levels distort the measurement even though plasma water tonicity is not low. These situations have different mechanisms and cannot be treated as routine hypotonic hyponatremia.

Verify the mechanism before targeting the number
Review glucose, osmolality, specimen quality, medications, fluids, kidney function, and the sodium trend. If the result is unexpected, assess the client and promptly clarify or repeat testing according to policy; do not delay emergency care when neurologic instability is present.

Hyponatremia causes water to enter brain cells

When extracellular fluid becomes hypotonic, water moves into cells. Brain swelling can produce headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion, gait change, lethargy, seizures, reduced consciousness, respiratory compromise, and herniation. Severity depends not only on the sodium value but also on how rapidly it fell, how low it is, and the client's vulnerabilities.

With gradual hyponatremia, brain cells adapt by releasing electrolytes and organic osmoles, reducing swelling. This adaptation protects brain volume but creates a different hazard: if chronic hyponatremia is corrected too rapidly, water can leave adapted cells faster than osmoles are restored, risking osmotic demyelination. The time course may be unclear, so prescribed limits and frequent monitoring matter.

Classify hypotonic hyponatremia by extracellular volume

Hypovolemic hyponatremia occurs when sodium and water are lost but sodium loss is proportionally greater or water is replaced without enough solute. Possible contexts include gastrointestinal losses, diuretics, skin losses, adrenal disorders, and renal salt loss. Cues may include postural symptoms, tachycardia, reduced perfusion, low urine output, and a history of loss.

Euvolemic hyponatremia usually reflects retained water without obvious edema. In syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, ADH action continues despite low plasma tonicity, limiting free-water excretion and leaving urine inappropriately concentrated. Pain, nausea, pulmonary or neurologic illness, malignancy, surgery, and several medications can contribute. Hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency are among conditions considered before attributing the pattern to SIADH.

Hypervolemic hyponatremia occurs when both sodium and water are increased but water gain is greater. Heart failure, advanced liver disease, and kidney failure can produce edema or ascites while reduced effective circulating volume continues to stimulate water-retaining pathways. Visible fluid excess and impaired perfusion can coexist.

Urine studies show the kidney's response

Urine osmolality helps show whether the kidney is excreting dilute water or retaining water under ADH influence. Urine sodium can help distinguish renal sodium handling from some extrarenal losses, but diuretics, kidney disease, recent fluids, dietary intake, and timing may alter the pattern. These results support a clinical interpretation; no single cutoff replaces the history and examination.

Record the timing of specimens relative to IV fluids, diuretics, vomiting, seizures, and other therapy. A sample collected after treatment may not represent the original physiology. Review trends rather than forcing discordant results into one label.

Severe symptomatic hyponatremia is an emergency

New seizure, profound confusion, obtundation, respiratory compromise, or rapidly worsening neurologic status requires immediate ABC assessment, emergency help, seizure precautions, and the organization's critical sodium pathway. Prescribed hypertonic saline may be used for severe symptoms with closely controlled dosing and repeated sodium measurement. It is a high-alert therapy; the RN verifies concentration, route, pump settings, compatibility, monitoring frequency, and escalation parameters.

Do not independently give large amounts of free water or sodium, change fluid restrictions, or accelerate an infusion. Treatment depends on symptoms, acuity, tonicity, volume status, cause, and risk for osmotic demyelination. Correction can accelerate unexpectedly after volume restoration or when ADH falls and a water diuresis begins.

Hypernatremia usually reflects too little water

Hypernatremia means water is insufficient relative to sodium. Common mechanisms include inadequate access to water, impaired thirst, gastrointestinal or insensible loss, osmotic diuresis, and excessive dilute urine from deficient ADH production or reduced kidney response. Sodium gain can also cause hypernatremia but is less common.

Clients at particular risk include infants, older adults, people with impaired consciousness or mobility, clients who cannot communicate thirst, and those with high ongoing water losses. A functioning thirst response protects many alert adults, so new hypernatremia should prompt assessment of access, cognition, swallowing safety, intake, urine volume, medications, and losses.

Hypernatremia causes brain-cell water loss

Hypertonic extracellular fluid draws water out of cells. Neurologic cues can include intense thirst, restlessness, irritability, weakness, confusion, twitching, seizures, and coma. Acute rises can cause more severe cellular shrinkage. With chronic hypernatremia, brain cells accumulate osmoles to restore volume; overly rapid lowering may then drive water into adapted cells and cause cerebral edema.

Polyuria with very dilute urine despite hypernatremia suggests impaired ADH production or renal response and requires prompt evaluation. Concentrated low-volume urine may instead indicate that the kidney is conserving water appropriately in response to extrarenal loss or inadequate intake. Kidney disease and diuretics can complicate either pattern.

Restore perfusion and tonicity in the correct sequence

A client with hypernatremia and shock may require prescribed isotonic volume resuscitation first because organ perfusion is immediately threatened, even though the client ultimately needs free-water replacement. Once circulation is stabilized, the care plan addresses the calculated water deficit, ongoing losses, route, and safe correction rate. Enteral water may be appropriate when ordered and swallowing or tube safety is established; IV fluid choice depends on the clinical situation.

The RN measures intake and output, urine amount and concentration, weight, neurologic status, vital signs, perfusion, glucose, sodium and other ordered laboratory values. Ongoing fever, diarrhea, drains, polyuria, or osmotic diuresis can make a static calculation inaccurate. Therapy is adjusted by the treating team using serial response, not by a one-time formula alone.

Medication and fluid history can reveal the cause

Review diuretics, antidepressants, antiseizure medications, desmopressin, glucocorticoids, IV solutions, tube-feeding water orders, bowel preparations, and nonprescription intake. Ask about recent surgery, pain, nausea, pulmonary or neurologic illness, endocrine disease, kidney disease, heart failure, liver disease, vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, and changes in thirst or urine output.

Water restriction is not a universal treatment for low sodium, and encouraging water is not automatically safe for every high sodium result. The same serum sodium value can arise from different physiology. Implement only the client-specific plan and continue reassessment.

Evaluate correction and detect complications

Neurologic improvement, stable breathing, improving perfusion, appropriate urine output, and a sodium trend within the prescribed target support benefit. Report a rise or fall faster than ordered, sudden high-volume dilute urine, worsening headache, vomiting, confusion, weakness, dysarthria, dysphagia, movement change, seizure, or declining consciousness immediately.

Osmotic demyelination symptoms may emerge after apparent initial improvement and can be delayed. Cerebral edema during overly rapid hypernatremia correction can present with neurologic deterioration or seizures. Continue ordered surveillance after the number begins to normalize; reaching a laboratory range is not the same as completing safe recovery.

Translate sodium disorders into clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify neurologic change, time course, glucose and osmolality, volume findings, intake and losses, urine pattern, medications, and access to water.
  2. Analyze cues: Confirm tonicity and determine whether the pattern is hypovolemic, euvolemic, or hypervolemic while considering ADH and kidney response.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Severe neurologic symptoms, airway risk, shock, and a rapidly changing sodium outrank routine etiologic workup.
  4. Generate solutions: Plan seizure safety, prescribed fluid or restriction, cause-directed care, accurate output measurement, serial laboratory checks, and escalation thresholds.
  5. Take action: Stabilize ABCs, activate emergency care when indicated, administer prescribed therapy with high-alert safeguards, and document timing.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess neurologic status, perfusion, urine pattern, sodium trajectory, treatment response, and evidence of overly rapid correction.

Clinical example

An older adult who depends on others for drinking becomes increasingly restless and confused after fever and poor intake. Sodium has risen rapidly, urine is scant and concentrated, and orthostatic symptoms are present. The RN recognizes hypertonicity plus probable extracellular volume deficit, assesses ABCs and perfusion, institutes fall and neurologic safety measures, reports the trend and ongoing losses, implements the prescribed staged fluid plan, and repeatedly evaluates mental status, circulation, urine output, respiratory tolerance, and sodium correction.
